sections.heading: Checking zero-coefficient relations in examples
paragraphs: Zeros are x-values with p(x)=0, so a graph zero is a meeting with the x-axis, including tangency. A monic quadratic with zeros r and s is (x−r)(x−s)=x²−(r+s)x+rs. For leading coefficient A≠0 multiply this whole expression by A. Quadratic zero sum is −B/A and product C/A; cubic sums and products follow expansion with signs retained.
Factorisation reverses expansion: a polynomial is expressed as a product whose multiplication recreates it.

sections.heading: Why the method works
paragraphs: For x²+sx+p, candidate constants a,b need both a+b=s and ab=p. One condition alone is insufficient. Regrouping also uses common factors: ax+ay+bx+by=a(x+y)+b(x+y)=(a+b)(x+y). A zero of a factored polynomial makes at least one factor zero.

Look for a common factor first, then use an identity or two-number sum/product search. Expand your proposed factors to check every coefficient. When the original expression is divided, retain exclusions from any cancelled denominator factors.

sections.heading: Check, remember and transfer
paragraphs: The middle coefficient must also match their sum. Always expand back.

sections.heading: Solving quadratics by factorisation
paragraphs: Put the equation in ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0. Factoring uses the zero-product property; completing the square yields x=(−b±√(b²−4ac))/(2a).
